analysis.one_liner: Requires giant social media platforms to let users move their data and connect across competitors.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by one Democrat, one Republican cosponsor, and another Democrat, never got a hearing or vote in the Senate Commerce Committee and died when the 116th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have forced the biggest social media and messaging platforms — those with more than 100 million U.S. monthly users — to build public doors into their systems: users could download or transfer their data to a rival app, rival apps could interoperate with the giant networks, and users could hire a registered third party to manage their accounts. The Federal Trade Commission would enforce the rules, counting each affected user as a separate violation when fining a platform, and the national standards agency would write model technical standards to make the connections work.
analysis.who_benefits: The hundreds of millions of people who use platforms like Facebook, Instagram, and Twitter, who today face high switching costs because their friends, photos, and history are locked inside one network. Smaller and startup communication apps also gain, because they could plug into the big networks' interfaces instead of building a user base from zero.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Users of big social media platforms

how_it_helps.text: Users could move their data — the information linked to them that platforms collect — to a competing service in a machine-readable format, making it far easier to leave a network without starting over.

Rival communication apps could connect interoperably with the giants, so a user on a small messaging app could reach friends on a platform like Facebook, weakening the network lock-in that keeps people on the biggest services.

Users could designate a registered 'custodial third-party agent' to manage their online interactions, content, and account settings on their behalf, with the FTC setting verification rules and the power to deregister agents that abuse access.

Enforcement had teeth: the FTC would treat violations as unfair or deceptive practices, assess compliance regularly, take complaints from users, and count each individual user affected by a violation as a separate violation when calculating fines.

The National Institute of Standards and Technology would publish model technical standards for interoperable messaging, multimedia sharing, and social networking within 180 days, and platforms using an open standard would get a presumption they were acting fairly.

analysis.who_pays: The handful of large platform providers above the 100-million-user threshold — Facebook, Google, Twitter and any similar service — which would bear the cost of building and maintaining open interfaces, documenting them, and giving up the network lock-in that keeps users from leaving. Third-party account managers could also charge users fees for their services.

drawbacks.text: Mandated doors into massive networks create real security and privacy risks: every competing provider that pulls user data becomes a potential leak point, and the bill only requires those providers to 'reasonably secure' the data they acquire.

Platforms could set usage thresholds and charge fees for high-volume access, proportional to their cost and risk — a lever a determined incumbent could use to slow or burden competitors even while nominally complying.

The third-party account managers the bill authorizes could charge users fees and would gain deep access to people's accounts; FTC registration, duties of loyalty, and deregistration powers are the only backstop against misuse.

The bill would take effect only after the FTC finished writing regulations, and the FTC's track record of moving slowly against large platforms meant the protections could be delayed or diluted in practice.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are real but diffuse: lower switching costs and more competition in services nearly every American uses, which would likely mean better products and less lock-in. The costs concentrate on a handful of companies with the resources to absorb them, though the security exposure from many new access points and the possibility of fee games are genuine weaknesses an honest supporter would concede. The bigger problem is that the bill never advanced far enough for any of this to be tested.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Commerce Committee never took the bill up after it was referred, and it died quietly when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Senator Mark Warner introduced the bill on October 22, 2019, with Republican Josh Hawley and Democrat Richard Blumenthal as original cosponsors, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation the same day.
That referral was the bill's only action: the record shows no hearing, no committee vote, no floor debate, and no roll call at any point in the 116th Congress.
The bill expired when the Congress ended on January 3, 2021, meaning all of its requirements — data portability, interoperability, and delegable accounts — never took effect.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The large platforms the bill targeted — Facebook, Google, Twitter and similar services — came out ahead: they never had to open their networks to competitors or give up the lock-in that keeps users on them.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was bipartisan from birth — a Democratic sponsor with one Republican and one Democratic cosponsor — but no chamber ever voted on it, so there is no vote record showing how the parties would have split.

industries.industry: Large social media and messaging platforms (Facebook, Google, Twitter)
industries.note: The bill's requirements fell only on platforms with over 100 million U.S. monthly users, forcing them to build open interfaces that would let users leave and competitors connect. Its core aim was to erode the network lock-in that is the foundation of their market power, so their interest ran directly against the bill's purpose — and their preference was served when the bill died in committee without a vote.

Rival providers would have gained documented access to interoperability interfaces and ported user data, letting them compete for users without rebuilding entire social graphs from scratch. Their fortunes rise only if ordinary users actually get the freedom to switch, so their interest runs alongside the public's.

The bill created a new licensed role — the custodial third-party agent — that could register with the FTC, manage users' accounts, and charge users fees for doing so. This would mint a new fee-charging intermediary industry, regulated by access duties and deregistration powers but still inserting a paid middleman between users and their data.
